Synthesize this into a cohesive paragraph: Type 2 diabetes mellites (T2DM) is a health burden with a rise in epidemic prevalence worldwide1. T2D is characterized by increased blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia)2. Metformin is the most-prescribed medication to treat patients with T2DM due to its glucose-lowering effects3. Metformin propagates insulin sensitivity by mainly reducing hepatic glucose production (through an activation of the hepatic AMP-activated protein kinase protein)4. The most common side effect of metformin is gastrointestinal discomfort, including diarrhea, nausea, flatulence and bloating5. There is growing evidence in animal and human studies suggesting that the gut microbiome is another target involved in the anti-diabetic effects of metformin6,7,8,9. Recent investigations documented the therapeutic benefit of orally-administrated metformin compared to intravenously-administrated metformin in T2D patients, suggesting the beneficial contribution of the gut microbiota10. Metformin alters the gut microbiome by enhancing Escherichia sp, Akkermansia muciniphila and Subdoligranuum variable; reducing Intestinibacter bartletti and increasing the levels of short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate and propionate7,8. This could indicate the anti-obesity property of metformin by modulating the gut microbiome and its metabolites. However, the precise mechanisms are unclear.

Understanding the role of bacterial-derived gut metabolites can provide a platform to elucidate interactions between microbe-microbe, microbe-diet and drugs. The gut microbiota is an attractive target for therapeutic intervention and using nutrition may help to promote drug efficiency and reduce gastrointestinal side effects11. To elucidate these interactions individual and systems-level analysis is needed12,13,14. Hence, systems biology approaches could be applied to reveal these associations between the abundances of different microbes and the molecular mechanisms underlying metformin treatment on a metabolic level15. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMS) have been used to gain a detailed understanding of microbial metabolic changes in various environments. Previous studies used GEMs to understand the metabolic interactions between microbes and host- microbes16,17,18.

Wu et al. 2017 collected fecal samples from treatment naïve individuals that received 1,700 mg/d metformin treatment (22 patients) for 4 months and generated shotgun metagenomics data to determine the species abundances7. In the present study we re-analyzed this metagenomics data with an updated gut microbial gene catalog and metagenome species profile19. We carried out further analysis by investigating carbohydrate-active enzymes of the significantly altered species. This analysis showed that species that are decreased after 4 months of metformin treatment have an increased number of annotated mucins and host glycan degradation in comparison to the significantly increased species. In addition, we performed constraint-based analysis using GEMS integrating different diets to predict the phenotype of the drug metformin on the human gut microbiota. These diet-microbiota interactions can help us understand how to increase drug efficiency or mimic drug effects in the gut microbiome of patients with a dysbiosis to an improved phenotype.

Chondroid Syringoma
Introduction:
A chondroid syringoma, or mixed tumor of the skin, has been described in individuals ranging in age from 20 to 70-years-old with a slight predilection for males. These lesions have been reported on the extremities, face, and neck [1]. Chondroid syringomas have been reported hundreds of times in the literature, however a hyaline cell-rich chondroid syringoma (HCRCS) to our knowledge has only been reported twelve times, this case being the thirteenth [2-4]. Although HCRCS tumors have been discussed a number of times throughout the literature there is a need to more readily recognize this often malignant appearing histology as a typically benign lesion [1,5-9].
 
Case Report:
Our patient was a 31-year-old male who presented with a 3.5 centimeter nodule on the vertex scalp (figure x). After examination, an excisional biopsy was performed and the specimen was sent for histological evaluation. Histology showed that many of the epithelioid cells were arranged in broad sheets and nests which also demonstrated a plasmacytoid appearance with an ovoid eccentric nucleus having fine granular chromatin and a deeply eosinophilic ′hyaline-like′ cytoplasm (figure y). Additionally, there were interconnecting tubuloalveolar structures lined by two layers of cuboidal epithelial cells, and ductal structures lined by one-to-two layered epithelial cells (figure z). This combination of features led to the diagnosis of a hyaline cell-rich chondroid syringoma of the scalp. This diagnosis is a rare, benign variant of a chondroid syringoma.
 
Discussion:
        	As can be seen in (figure a), atypical cells are present in the lesion. However, there are a myriad of more reassuring features present as well, and these overwhelmingly reassuring features are what drives the diagnosis. The benign features include smooth tumor borders, good circumscription of the tumor, a predominance of bland cells, and a lack of mitotic figures throughout the specimen. While these portions of this tumor ultimately led to the correct diagnosis of a benign lesion, the atypical portions should not be dismissed quickly because of the concern they present for possible malignant neoplasms. The atypical cells seen here can be similar to the histologies found in malignant melanoma, myxoid chondrosarcoma, and alveolar soft part sarcoma.
        	Melanoma is rightly in the differential diagnosis because of the similarities with hyaline-cell-rich chondroid syringoma in regards to the plasmacytoid characteristics shown by both diagnoses. Melanomas will typically contain a junctional component, melanin, and are infiltrative, all characteristics not seen in HCRCS. Melanomas can have myxoid stroma similar to HCRCS. However, HCRCS will display duct structures and cartilage, and these features would not be expected to be present in melanoma [10].
        	Myxoid chondrosarcoma is an additional tumor that can be easily confused with HCRCS. Both pathologies have the potential to show a lobulated or multinodular pattern, as well as chondroid areas and myxoid stroma containing small, rounded cells. Histological evaluation of myxoid chondrosarcomas are typically patterned in cords whereas HCRCS have a tendency to display a nest or sheet pattern [10]. Each tumor has the potential to be in the subcutaneous tissue, but HCRCS are more likely to be found in this location. Myxoid chondrosarcomas, on the other hand, tend to locate to deep tissues, and can even involve muscles, tendons, and ligaments [10].
        	 Alveolar soft part sarcomas are characterized histologically by well-defined nests of cells separated by a fibrous stroma. The alveolar pattern arises from discohesive cells and there are rarely mitotic figures, but vascular invasion is common with characteristic rod-shaped crystalloids. Additionally, large polygonal cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli are present [11].

Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Disparaging epithets are often attributed to the “non-West,” reinforcing connotations of inferiority, irrationality, belligerence, otherness, fanaticism, and barbarism in comparison to the West. This belief in Western superiority is often reinforced through various forms of discourse, including history, literature, art, music, etc. In a similar vein, through the utilization of Eurocentric and imperialistic perspectives, academic discourse has consistently depicted ‘Eastern societies’ as exotic and racialized, perpetuating a biased portrayal of the Orient or East.

Volunteers will need to sort the books into categories and arrange them in an inviting way, like at a bookstore. Books should be inexpensive, so people buy more—maybe fifty cents for paperbacks and two dollars for hardcover books. A book sale would appeal to people of all ages, from little kids to the elderly.
